I just re-ran the full test suite natively on both Windows and Linux to verify the new opcode memory alignments, and everything is perfectly stable just in case. Happy to make any architectural adjustments if needed! For reference about testing, I'll attach the script I used and it's output and error logs below. 1) script: ``` extends Node class testNode extends Node: var payload: String = "active" func get_self() -> testNode: return self func test() -> testNode: # free() does not wait for the end of the frame like queue_free(). # It instantly destroys the C++ memory, turning 'self' into a zombie pointer. free() return self func _ready(): var null_trap: testNode = null var live_trap: testNode = testNode.new() # TEST 1: The Phantom Assignment # Tests: OPCODE_SET_NAMED_SAFE # If this crashes, the SET opcode isn't properly evaluating Variant::NIL null_trap?.payload = "hacked" print("Test 1 (Phantom Assignment) Passed. This snippet crashes, making the feature pretty much useless with static typing. `print(i)` does not crash, but assigns and prints null (i'd say that's a different issue) ``` extends Node func _ready() -> void: var i: int = get_node_or_null("InvalidPath")?.process_priority print(i) var n: String = get_node_or_null("InvalidPath")?.name print(n) ```
Yeah, null safe access requires an elvis/null coalescing operator to be useful in practice, I'd say

Implementing an elvis operator will probably proof hard with the current analyzer. While for `?.` setting the type to `Variant` is a quick solution for typed code, there is no simple way to revert the downgrade since we loose all information about the original type as well.

Implementing this would require nullable types (internally) I guess.

@HolonProduction I think I might understand what you mean. I know that `?.` drops the expression to a Variant, the analyzer goes blind to the original type. In that scenario, the analyzer forgets the original type and the downgraded Variant acts like a black box effectively making it impossible for the elvis operator `?:` (say) to compute the complex union types and assign the right value. Please do correct me if I'm getting this wrong.

But If my hypothesis is correct, I was thinking what if we completely bypass the analyzer's limitations by treating the Elvis operator as an automated boilerplate? Like, instead of trying to teach the type checker how to resolve a Variant back into a strict type, what if the parser just treats A ?: B as a shortcut and silently expands it into a standard ternary operation behind the scenes before the analyzer even sees it?

For example, consider:
`var final_name: String = player?.get_name() ?: "Default string"`

The parser could just automatically unpack that into a hidden structure like:
```
var __tmp_1 = player?.get_name()
var final_name: String = __tmp_1 if __tmp_1 != null else "Default string"
```

This way, we just might be able to bypass the static analyzer problem. It already knows perfectly how to strictly type-check a standard if/else block. The temporary variable absorbs the Variant downgrade from the left side, and the ternary safely guarantees the strict String fallback for the final assignment (We'd just have to make sure we use that hidden temporary variable so we don't accidentally evaluate the left side twice, in case it's a function call).

Do you think a boilerplate generation approach like this could be a viable workaround to get the Elvis operator working without needing the internal nullable types (for now atleast)?
I would say it is far easier to have the type checker acknowledge chain types than generate gdscript code under the hood a la macros...

Not sure what you mean by "chain type".

If I understand the makro like approach right, you suggest that the elvis OP evaluates to `Variant` on a type level? That would make it unusable with inference `:=`. It also would mark a lot of lines as unsafe which is absolutely counterintuitive for code that is meant to be null-safe.

It would also probably prevent the compiler from generating typed OP's when the elvis OP is part of a complex expression.

@HolonProduction You're completely right. I was brainstorming a macro/desugaring workaround at the parser level and some other alternatives just to see if we could avoid the Variant downgrade, but all routes seem to ultimately break the type inference (:=) and disabling typed instructions is a dealbreaker. As much as I'd love to implement the Elvis operator alongside this, I understand now that faking it creates unsafe side effects and bad editor UX. Like C# or Kotlin, it really does need true internal nullable types to work correctly without destroying static type safety. And correspondingly without the Elvis OP the `?.` isn't essentially the most useful. Since rewriting the analyzer's core to support internal nullables is a massive structural headache, I think it's best we convert this PR into a draft for now. Keeping its scope strictly focused on the `?.` safe navigation operator, which successfully evaluates to Variant and safely prevents the runtime crashes. (Also, I ran some VM stress tests on the current ?. implementation and confirmed it doesn't double-evaluate the left-hand side. Functions with side-effects only trigger exactly once, and the VM stack stays perfectly aligned! Please find the used script the output logs at the end of this comment!) Happy to make any final adjustments to the ?. implementation if you guys spot anything else! Script: ``` extends Node var evaluation_count: int = 0 func get_enemy(): evaluation_count += 1 return null func _ready(): # Test 1: Single execution get_enemy()?.take_damage() if evaluation_count == 1: print("Success: LHS evaluated exactly once! No double-evaluation.") else: print("Failure: LHS evaluated ", evaluation_count, " times.") # Test 2: Stack Integrity (10,000 executions) for i in range(10000): var _x = get_enemy()?.some_property # 1 + 10000 = 10001 if evaluation_count == 10001: print("Success") else: print("Failure: Total evaluations were ", evaluation_count) ``` Output:
